title: Maintaining
hook: keeping good states going and growing

segments.voice: Yesterday: arousing, and your line, wake the good. Did you start one good habit, and do it once? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

Day one of a new habit has the thrill of starting. Day two is just doing it again. No fanfare, no new pen. A beautiful journal gets three lovely pages, and six months later it turns up under the bed, the rest of it blank. Starting a good thing is the third effort. Keeping it going is the fourth, and for this one the Buddha reached for pictures from the farmyard and the workshop. Today: maintaining.
screen: `DAY ONE: THE THRILL.` → `DAY TWO: AGAIN.` → `THE JOURNAL UNDER THE BED.`

segments.voice: The fourth effort, in the Numbered Discourses, is for wholesome states that have already arisen: you work to keep them, so they don't fade or get muddled, and to help them grow and come to fullness. The Pali name is anurakkhaṇā, protecting, guarding what you have. In the list's own example, it's a meditator protecting a steady object of concentration once they've found it. But how do you keep at something without straining? A sutta in the Connected Discourses gives two pictures. A hen sits on her eggs, eight or ten or twelve. She covers them, warms them, tends them properly. She doesn't need to wish, may my chicks break out today. If she keeps sitting, they will. Then a carpenter looks at the handle of his adze, a woodworking tool, and sees the marks his fingers have worn into it. He couldn't tell you how much wore away today, or yesterday. But it wore. Practice is like that, the Buddha says: a monk can't see how much of the mind's taints wore away today, but steady practice wears them away. That's the spirit of maintaining. Not dramatic. Not checking every hour. Just sitting on the eggs. The Dhammapada adds the other half, in Max Müller's words: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good." Do it again, and enjoy it. Gladness isn't a distraction from keeping a good thing going. It's part of what keeps it going.
screen: `ANURAKKHAṆĀ: GUARDING WHAT'S GROWN.` · `THE HEN ON HER EGGS.` · `THE WORN ADZE HANDLE.` · `DO IT AGAIN, AND ENJOY IT.` · then, large: `KEEP IT GOING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring back the good habit you started yesterday, or any good thing you've been doing lately. Don't measure it. Don't ask whether it's working. Just picture yourself doing it again today, the way a hen settles back onto her eggs: no fuss, no wishing, simply returning. Let a little gladness come with the picture, if it wants to. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maintaining. Anurakkhaṇā, the fourth effort: keeping good states going and growing, like a hen sitting on her eggs.
Your line: keep it going. Today, continue yesterday's good once more, and let yourself enjoy it. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners keep daily routines, a morning sit, evening chanting, regular offerings, and many traditions encourage rejoicing in one's own good deeds as a way of sustaining them.

fork.setup: you're a hen with a clutch of eggs. by SN 22.101, what gets the chicks out?
fork.reveal: the Buddha says a hen who covers and warms her eggs properly needn't wish for the chicks to hatch; they will. steady practice works the same way.

original.note: Pali anurakkhaṇā: protecting, guarding; the fourth right effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: keeping a habit takes iron discipline.
what it means: steady, unfussy returning, like a hen on her eggs, with some gladness in it.
what a scholar hears: SN 22.101 pairs the hen and the adze-handle similes to say progress is real even when it can't be seen day by day; AN 4.14 names the fourth effort anurakkhaṇā.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: removed sweeping hook claims ('day two of anything is harder', 'every gym knows') and the superlative 'most patient pictures'; the adze-handle simile now says what wears away in SN 22.101 (the taints, āsavas), which the earlier line left vague.
Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 118 in SBE 10.
SN 22.101 paraphrased (hen with eight, ten or twelve eggs; carpenter's adze handle). The same hen simile also appears in MN 16 and AN 7.71. Confirm numbering.
AN 4.14's example for anurakkhaṇā (guarding an arisen concentration sign, e.g. the perception of a skeleton) is summarized without the specific perceptions.
